source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Models were told that a wrong answer costs a penalty. They almost never changed whether they answered or abstained. Rudner's point (move the acceptance threshold with the cost of error) is not met by default.
numbers: Penalties 0 to 100 in the prompt; optimal threshold is lambda/(1+lambda) (about 0.99 at penalty 100). Models: GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2 (+Thinking), Qwen3-Next-80B, Gemini-2.5/3-Flash, Gemma-3n-E4B, Llama-4-Maverick. Sets: HLE, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K.
quote: Even when extreme penalties render frequent abstention the mathematically optimal strategy, models almost never abstain
limits: Penalty is set in a prompt, not a real cost; abstain option only; verbal confidence is the model's own.
agent_relevance: Abstain rules must be enforced by code, not left to the model's reading of stakes. Put a stake-dependent threshold in the program.

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Policy consistency (decision matches the optimal rule for the model's own stated confidence) is high at low penalties, then collapses.
numbers: High consistency at penalty <=5; sharp drop at penalty >=10 on HLE and GPQA. On HLE averaged over penalty >=10: policy consistency 0.119 (DeepSeek-V3.2-Think) to 0.492 (Qwen3-Next-Think); normalized utility with own policy -0.295 to -0.862 across models.
limits: Averages over the high-penalty regime only; HLE is hard so errors are many.
agent_relevance: Model behaviour is not a smooth threshold curve; it turns unstable. Do not trust the model to apply a risk threshold itself.

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Confidence is informative but unused. Applying the optimal threshold in code on the model's own verbal confidence gives large utility gains.
numbers: HLE, penalty >=10: normalized utility gain from code-enforced threshold +0.313 (GPT-5-nano) to +0.685 (Llama-4-Maverick); e.g. DeepSeek-V3.2 -0.853 to -0.169; Llama-4-Maverick -0.688 to -0.004.
limits: Gain is computed under the model's stated belief, not true correctness; HLE ECE is high (0.47 to 0.85), so the real gain is smaller.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the schema split: program holds the threshold, model only supplies a confidence slot. Cheap scaffold, large measured effect.

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Telling models to use their confidence to decide whether to answer did not help.
numbers: Appended directive to use the confidence to decide whether to answer or abstain; abstention and regret curves matched baseline; policy-consistency shift near zero across benchmarks.
limits: Single prompt wording; reasoning effort not varied.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only stake instructions are weak; use code gates (the escalation paper, c08, shows the exception when reasoning is on).

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Higher penalties did not change accuracy or stated confidence. The model's confidence is not cost-aware either.
numbers: Answer accuracy and reported confidence flat across penalty 0.1 to 100.
limits: Same limits as c01.
agent_relevance: Stakes do not change belief; only a threshold step turns belief into a cost-aware action.

source: DosSantos DiSorbo et al. (2026) Act or Escalate? Evaluating Escalation Behavior in Automation with Language Models
finding: Escalate-versus-implement is a Rudner-style decision. The optimal threshold is 1 - c/cw (cost of escalating over cost of a wrong action). Models have very different implicit thresholds, not set by size or family.
numbers: Eight models, five domains. Implicit threshold p* about 53-54% (GPT-5-mini, low) to over 91% (GPT-5-nano 91%, Llama 4 Maverick 92%). Qwen3.5-9B 56% vs Qwen3.5-397B 81%; GPT-5-nano 91% vs GPT-5-mini 53%.
quote: Neither behavior is inherently correct; the optimal threshold depends on the cost ratio R.
limits: Threshold fitted by linear regression of escalation rate on a given accuracy signal; domains are recorded human decisions.
agent_relevance: Measure the agent's own threshold before deployment; the default error-cost weighting is a hidden value judgment.

source: DosSantos DiSorbo et al. (2026) Act or Escalate? Evaluating Escalation Behavior in Automation with Language Models
finding: Models are mostly overconfident about their own accuracy, and self-belief does not predict the threshold.
numbers: 304 model x condition pairs: 201 (66%) overconfident. Self-estimates 76% (Llama 3.3 70B) to 97% (Mixtral 8x7B) vs actual 75-80%. GPT-5-mini: mean 80% vs actual 78%, but per-condition gaps -38 to +27 points.
limits: Self-estimate inferred from the no-signal escalation rate.
agent_relevance: Calibration and decision threshold are two separate things to measure; fixing one does not fix the other.

source: DosSantos DiSorbo et al. (2026) Act or Escalate? Evaluating Escalation Behavior in Automation with Language Models
finding: Prompting with the cost ratio works only together with reasoning. Fine-tuning on an explicit expected-cost chain of thought gives near-perfect decisions.
numbers: Qwen3.5-9B accuracy vs optimal action at R=4 (threshold 75%): baseline 62.0%, +cost framing 63.9%, +thinking 61.9%, +both 78.8%. GPT-5-mini: 64.7%; +cost 75.8%; +reasoning 73.2%; +both 87.1%. SFT on a CoT template (expected cost of implementing = R x Y compared to 1): 100% on all datasets and cost ratios 2 to 50, 100% on held-out MovieLens; about 84% when the signal is removed.
limits: SFT model trained on the same template it is tested on; one 9B model; the signal gives accuracy directly.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for an explicit worked step (state cost ratio, compute threshold, compare) inside a reasoning mode. Fits the 'model fills a slot, program decides' split.

source: Yamin, Kelly, Wilder, Horvitz (2026) High-Stakes Decisions with Language Models: Insights from Emergency Triage
finding: Default under-triage is mostly an implicit cost weighting, not weak ranking. Models rank cases well but differ in where they put the threshold.
numbers: AUROC 0.95-0.99 for all models on the emergency endpoint. Default GPT-5-mini reasoning: false alarm about 10%, catches only about 48% of true emergencies; other families catch 94-100% with false alarms 12-28%. 576 variants (64 emergencies) for the original endpoint; 1,248 variants for the expanded set.
quote: Deploying a model with no stated priority therefore means accepting an implicit value judgment that is both unobservable in advance and variable.
limits: Cannot reproduce the deployed ChatGPT Health exactly; the deployed tool sits below the frontier implied by the model's own probabilities.
agent_relevance: A direct computational case of Douglas: the default threshold embeds a value choice nobody stated. The agent should state its error-cost assumption.

source: Yamin, Kelly, Wilder, Horvitz (2026) High-Stakes Decisions with Language Models: Insights from Emergency Triage
finding: Stating the cost ratio moves the operating point along the ROC curve for capable models.
numbers: Cost ratios 5 or 10 (missed emergency vs unneeded referral) on GPT-5-mini reasoning: share of true emergencies routed up about 50% with no rise in unnecessary referrals (original endpoint), about 30% on the extended endpoint; prompts span most of the ROC curve, near 100% sensitivity.
limits: Gain depends on reasoning mode and capability.
agent_relevance: Cost-ratio prompts do work when the model can reason; contrast with c01-c04.

source: Yamin, Kelly, Wilder, Horvitz (2026) High-Stakes Decisions with Language Models: Insights from Emergency Triage
finding: Steering fidelity depends on capability and reasoning. Claude models shift the right way but dampened at the extremes.
numbers: GPT-5.4 follows prompted utilities even at minimal reasoning; GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek with reasoning off stay in a narrow threshold range despite large prompt changes. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 shift correctly across reasoning levels, but recovered ratios span a narrower range, mainly at 0.1 or 100 times. Stating the probability threshold directly gives similar results.
limits: Cost ratio range 0.1 to 100; model-specific.
agent_relevance: Test steering per model. At extreme stakes, prompts under-deliver; a code-level threshold is safer.

source: Yamin, Kelly, Wilder, Horvitz (2026) High-Stakes Decisions with Language Models: Insights from Emergency Triage
finding: An external fixed threshold on elicited probabilities is a robust alternative to prompting.
numbers: Best fixed utility ratio recovered per model; each target ratio maps to a model-specific probability threshold; compensates for miscalibration; agreement with prompted regimes 80-100% across models.
limits: Needs reviewed cases to set the threshold.
agent_relevance: Supports the design: elicit a probability, apply a program-held threshold chosen by the stakes tier.

source: Liu, Ding, Barrett et al. (2026) Misaligned Clinical Risk Classification and Cost Asymmetry in Open-Weight LLMs
finding: Models encode risk and cost direction internally but mostly do not use cost to shift decisions the right way.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B/32B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B; 11 FN:FP cost ratios (20:1 to 1:20), 3 phrasings; Pima diabetes vignettes. Risk probe AUC about 0.83. Only 2 of 12 model-phrasings passed the mirror test (opposite responses to rising FN vs FP cost with cost-correct ordering): 70B-original FN delta +0.713 (99.9% of patients moved right), FP -0.244 (78.6%); 32B-original +0.459 and -0.672.
quote: LLMs encode risk and cost information but do not reliably integrate them into cost-correct decisions.
limits: Small open models, one tabular dataset, greedy decoding; response to cost magnitude mostly direction-agnostic (shared component 68-94%).
agent_relevance: Represented but not used: a probe or a program must carry the threshold. Do not assume a stated cost shifts a small model correctly.

source: Liu, Ding, Barrett et al. (2026) Misaligned Clinical Risk Classification and Cost Asymmetry in Open-Weight LLMs
finding: A symmetric 1:1 tradeoff statement alone pushed every model toward the LOW-risk answer.
numbers: Median per-patient displacement in family-sum log-odds: -0.375 (Qwen-7B), -0.250 (Llama-8B), -0.375 (Qwen-32B), -1.125 (Llama-70B). Llama-3.1-8B tradeoff-free operating point FPR 0.51, TPR 0.88.
limits: Wording effect; one dataset.
agent_relevance: Merely mentioning costs can bias toward inaction; the wording of stakes is itself a lever to control.

source: Wu, Gustafsson, Phillips et al. (2026) BAS: A Decision-Theoretic Approach to Evaluating LLM Confidence
finding: A metric scoring answer-or-abstain utility across a range of risk thresholds. It penalizes confident errors much more than log loss does. Models with equal accuracy or ECE can differ a lot in BAS.
numbers: Twelve LLMs; AIME: GPT-4o 11.7% accuracy with BAS -5.06; GPT-oss 75.0% accuracy with BAS 0.57. On SimpleQA all models have negative BAS and ECE 49.0% to 84.2%. Larger and more accurate models tend to have higher BAS.
limits: Self-reported confidence; uniform prior over risk thresholds by default.
agent_relevance: Score the agent's accept/abstain behaviour with a stakes-weighted metric, not accuracy alone.

source: Wu, Gustafsson, Phillips et al. (2026) BAS: A Decision-Theoretic Approach to Evaluating LLM Confidence
finding: Cheap fixes help: top-k confidence elicitation and post-hoc calibration raise decision-level reliability.
numbers: Top-k (k=3) elicitation gave the highest BAS across models; isotonic regression on a held-out validation set reduces the penalty from overconfident errors.
limits: Needs validation data for the isotonic step.
agent_relevance: Elicit several candidate answers with confidences; calibrate on held-out items before applying the threshold.

source: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala, Zhang (2025) Why Language Models Hallucinate
finding: Binary grading makes abstaining strictly worse than a guess, so training and benchmarks reward over-acceptance of claims. Fix: state a confidence target t in the task, with mistakes penalized t/(1-t).
numbers: Examples t=0.5 (penalty 1), t=0.75 (penalty 2), t=0.9 (penalty 9). Argues for adding explicit confidence targets to mainstream evals.
quote: Answer only if you are > t confident, since mistakes are penalized t/(1 - t) points
limits: Theory plus argument; the threshold choice is arbitrary and social, not derived.
agent_relevance: This is Rudner's threshold made explicit. The agent prompt can state a target t per stakes tier; see c01-c04 on whether models obey.

source: Mohri, Hashimoto (2024) Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
finding: Break an output into sub-claims, score each, and drop the least certain until a chosen error rate alpha is guaranteed. The user picks the error budget; a value choice becomes a parameter.
numbers: Correctness guarantees 80-90%. Base to guaranteed: 30% to 80% FActScore, 78% to 93% NaturalQuestions, 75% to 95% MATH. Frequency scoring: FActScore factuality 25% to 80% while keeping about half of claims; NQ +15% by removing about a quarter; MATH +15% removing 10%. GPT-4.
limits: Guarantee is marginal, not conditional on topic; an imperfect scorer removes true claims; most examples lose 50% of claims at alpha 0.2 on FActScore.
agent_relevance: A ready-made inductive-risk mechanism: set alpha by the stakes tier, filter claims by score, report what was dropped.

source: Candes et al. (2024) Large language model validity via enhanced conformal prediction methods
finding: Follow-up to c18: notes the guarantee is not conditionally valid and that filtering can remove many accurate claims; proposes conditional and level-adaptive methods.
numbers: Not read this session; from a search summary only.
limits: Unverified details.
agent_relevance: Check before using conditional claim filtering at different stakes levels.

source: Rubin-Toles et al. (2025) Conformal Language Model Reasoning with Coherent Factuality
finding: Filters claims in a reasoning chain over a dependency graph so kept claims stay deducible.
numbers: About 90% factuality while keeping 80% or more of claims on MATH and FELM (search summary only).
limits: Not opened; figures from a summary.
agent_relevance: Relevant if the agent filters steps of a proof rather than isolated claims.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama, Neiswanger (2025) DeLLMa: Decision Making Under Uncertainty with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: A scaffold: the LLM lists unknown states and gives probabilities, a utility function is elicited by pairwise preference and fitted with Bradley-Terry, then code picks the action with highest expected utility. It beats zero-shot, CoT and self-consistency.
numbers: Up to 40% accuracy gain over baselines, larger when actions are many. Tested on agriculture and stock-investment decisions. Utility via Rank2Pairs or one-vs-all.
limits: 'Up to' figure; two domains with historical data; utility is elicited from the LLM, so values are the model's guess, not the stakeholder's.
agent_relevance: Closest published agent-loop method turning stated costs into a decision by code. Utilities should come from the user or a stakes table, not from the model.

source: Birch (2023) Medical AI, Inductive Risk, and the Communication of Uncertainty: Disorders of Consciousness
finding: Worked inductive-risk case for ML. Values on missed vs misattributed responsiveness shape the choice of significance threshold, correction method and false-discovery control.
numbers: Claassen et al. 2019 NEJM: 16 of 104 patients (15%) classed as cognitive-motor dissociation; authors note about 5 of the 16 likely statistical flukes, so expected false discovery rate about 5/16 = 0.31. Bonferroni controls per-patient misattribution but raises false negatives; Benjamini-Hochberg controls FDR but per-patient misattribution risk grows with the number of recordings.
limits: Philosophy draft; one clinical domain; not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Shows why 'accept at p<0.05' is a hidden value choice; the agent should pick its correction method by which error is worse.

source: Karaca (2021) Values and inductive risk in machine learning modelling: the case of binary classification models
finding: Argues ML classifier construction is underdetermined by data, so modellers must set error costs (a cost matrix) from social values. Cost-insensitive training maximizes accuracy; cost-sensitive training does not.
numbers: Credit example: Cost-1 (rejecting a low-risk applicant) and Cost-2 (accepting a high-risk applicant) must differ; their ratio moves the threshold. Cites Elkan (2001) cost-sensitive learning.
limits: Conceptual paper with a worked example, no benchmark numbers.
agent_relevance: The cost matrix is where values enter. Make it an explicit, logged input to the agent.

source: Biddle (2020) On Predicting Recidivism: Epistemic Risk, Tradeoffs, and Values in Machine Learning
finding: Values enter ML at problem framing, data choice and algorithm design, with tradeoffs between error types.
numbers: Search summary only; three recommendations for penal use.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Values enter at the framing step, not only at the threshold.

source: Chaudhary, Vega, Sharif, Narodytska, Singh (2025) LLM Representations for Enhanced Asymmetric Error Classification
finding: Plain LLM classifiers are suboptimal when one error is costlier. Neyman-Pearson linear probes on residual-stream states cap the costly error at a user threshold.
numbers: Tasks: medical QA, safety moderation, schema linking. Type-I error generally below 10%; average Type-I reduction from the original LLM classifier 34%. Best probes use middle to final layers. The same probe is reused with a new threshold; only the cut changes.
limits: Needs labelled training data and white-box access; not applicable to API-only models.
agent_relevance: Where internals are available, a cost-constrained probe is a sturdier gate than a prompt. For API agents, copy the idea with a held-out calibration set.

source: Rathkopf (2025) From Hallucination to Reliability: Generative Modeling and the Structure of Scientific Inference
finding: Philosophy of science view: separates 'corrosive' hallucinations (those that threaten reliability) from harmless ones, and argues risk can be managed in theoretically mature domains.
numbers: No numbers. The term inductive risk does not appear in the opened PDF text.
limits: Conceptual; no experiment.
agent_relevance: Weight claims by how corrosive an error would be, not all errors equally.

source: Li, Yi, Chen (2025) Beyond Accuracy: Rethinking Hallucination and Regulatory Response in Generative AI
finding: Legal analysis warns that treating hallucination only as an accuracy defect hides who bears the cost; no use of inductive-risk framing.
numbers: No numbers. The term inductive risk was not found in the opened text.
limits: Legal scholarship; not empirical.
agent_relevance: Search gap: no paper found that maps Rudner or Douglas directly onto LLM outputs.

source: Sullivan (2022) Inductive Risk, Understanding, and Opaque Machine Learning Models
finding: Philosophy paper on inductive risk for opaque ML models; listed in search results.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Possible follow-up on how opacity changes who can judge the threshold.
